extracted.intended_audience: mathematics department faculty, calculus instructors, and department chairs planning or assessing calculus instruction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and a questionnaire for assessing and initiating departmental discussion about goals, expectations, pedagogy, technology, and assessment practices in first-year undergraduate calculus courses. Includes specific survey items and recommended assessment tools and uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use questionnaires to initiate departmental discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use items from the CCH EDP questionnaires as a vehicle for beginning discussions about possible change in teaching calculus or for assessing changes already made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions may be used as the basis for instructor or full-department meetings (with or without prior completion), modified for local situations, administered anonymously before meetings, collated and analyzed, and distributed to stimulate conversation and inform decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt questionnaire items to local situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify items to develop a questionnaire more suited to your own situation or to include fewer or more comment-type questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation of reform should differ at each institution because patterns reflect local student needs, faculty attitudes, and institutional characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and distribute analyzed responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Have faculty complete the survey (anonymously if desired), collate and analyze responses, then distribute quantitative analyses and comment listings prior to discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distributing analyses helps focus departmental meetings and provides a starting point for formal discussions; responses to each set of items can serve as foundations for more formal instructor or department discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content: set level of emphasis on specific first-year topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate desired level of emphasis for a list of specific topics in a first-year calculus course (scale provided). Topics include preliminaries, limits, derivative concepts, definition-based derivatives, differentiation techniques, applications of derivatives, Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, definite integral as area, integration techniques, applications of integration, exponential/logarithmic applications, differential equations and applications, series and convergence, Taylor series and applications, parametrizations and vectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey uses a 1–5 scale (little or none to heavy). There is also space to add other topics or remarks concerning content; technology is addressed separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical methodology: emphasize methods in instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate level of emphasis to place on methods such as formal definitions, statements of theorems/counterexamples, proofs of significant theorems, historical themes, writing assignments, student practice of routine procedures, real-world applications, and analysis/solution of non-routine problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents rate emphasis on a 1–5 scale and are asked to reflect on how much emphasis they place on these items in assessment of students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and set an appropriate level of mathematical rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty should state their own definition of 'mathematical rigor' and describe what level is appropriate in first-year calculus and how they would assess it (e.g., grading criteria).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-ended responses capture local norms and guide consistency in expectations and grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology role and integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulate feelings about the role of technology in promoting or hindering learning, and indicate the extent to which technology should be integrated throughout the course versus used for special projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey provides specific options (calculators for numerical/graphing/symbolic, computer courseware such as Maple/Mathematica, modifying existing programs, spreadsheets) to be rated on a 1–5 emphasis scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom teaching approaches: frequency of instructional systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate how frequently students should use systems such as lecture notes as basis for learning, specially designed calculus laboratory, concrete materials/equipment, small group work on problems, small-group multi-class projects, in-class practice of procedures, and making conjectures/exploring multiple solution methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a frequency scale (not frequent to very frequent) and provide comments about the 'ideal classroom' and needed departmental supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student assessment/evaluation: weight course components
rubrics_metrics.description: State importance to course grade assigned to items such as quizzes/tests/exams, final exam, individual mastery tests, small-group tests, lab reports (individual/group), lab-related quizzes/tests, homework (individual/group), projects (individual/group), journals, class participation, portfolios, and other methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents rate importance on a scale and circle methods they wish to discuss in department meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspectives on calculus reform: awareness, positives, concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess faculty awareness of calculus reform issues and efforts, what they find encouraging about reform directions, and their concerns about those directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-ended prompts invite reflective responses to guide departmental policy and address misconceptions or resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit perspectives on current text
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask faculty to comment on the current text in use and whether they want to change it, with explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text choice is connected to departmental goals, student needs, and reform activities; use responses to inform curricular decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit perspectives on current students
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect faculty impressions of the most recent calculus class taught and any student comments they wish to pass on to the department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these qualitative insights to inform changes in support, pedagogy, and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop pedagogy: learner-centered interactive instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt an interactive, hands-on Workshop approach where instructors introduce ideas briefly and intuitively, then let students work collaboratively on learner-centered tasks before formalizing theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor mingles with students, guides discussion, poses questions, encourages productive struggle, and gives mini-lectures only after reflection; tasks include computer tasks, written exercises, and classroom activities to promote observation, connection-making, and communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize conceptual understanding before procedural skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach what an idea is (e.g., what a derivative is and when it is useful) before teaching how to perform procedures (e.g., differentiation rules); encourage students to write about their observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baseline data and pre/post testing indicated improved conceptual explanations (e.g., increase from small fraction to ~80% correct descriptions after activities). Writing/journals are used routinely to monitor conceptual gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect baseline data on student understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Before implementing changes, collect baseline information about students' understanding of fundamental concepts (e.g., 'What is a derivative?') to identify needs and track changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use baseline results to justify emphasis changes (e.g., need for conceptual emphasis and writing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administer pre- and post-tests to measure learning gains
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask students questions before activities and re-ask later to measure conceptual gains (e.g., functions described before and after unit activities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare responses to quantify improvement and refine instructional materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze student journal entries for insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Require end-of-unit journal reflections asking students to describe learned concepts, what was easy/hard, what helped, and suggested revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals provide instructors with insight into students' understanding and candid feedback about what works and what doesn't; use to revise units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative test questions for external benchmarking
rubrics_metrics.description: Include questions from external exams (e.g., Penn/USNA items) to compare performance to students at other institutions using similar or different materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative items can validate curriculum effectiveness relative to other programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct structured critical interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview representative students in structured ways to determine their thinking processes, categorize responses, transcribe interviews, and analyze results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical interviews reveal specific conceptual misunderstandings (e.g., limited view of definite integral) and inform task revisions in activity guides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use end-of-semester attitudinal questionnaires
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask students to rate effectiveness of activities, perceived gains in understanding, changes in attitudes toward mathematics, and comfort with technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze responses (including gender differences) to assess affective outcomes and perceived usefulness of course components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather follow-up longitudinal data
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect data one or two years post-course on attitudes, continuation in mathematics (e.g., enrollment in Calc II), performance in subsequent courses, choice of major, and use of calculus in other departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow-up data is used to determine longer-term impact of course reforms on attitudes and academic outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine quantitative and qualitative assessment methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use both objective quantitative measures (e.g., final exam scores, pre/post-tests) and rich qualitative methods (observations, interviews, journals) to get a complete picture of student learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative data provides broad measures; qualitative data yields insights into student thinking and guidance for course improvement. Using them in tandem fine-tunes course delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: State clear intended outcomes and design supportive assessment tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a clear statement of intended outcomes, design assessment tools that support those outcomes, and analyze and summarize results accessibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summaries should be easy to understand (e.g., bar charts or graphs) to communicate findings to faculty, administrators, funders, and students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a variety of assessment measures (prismatic assessment lens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ multiple assessment measures (pre/post-tests, journals, interviews, comparative questions, attitudinal surveys, follow-up studies) to explore issues from different angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple measures often raise new questions but bring departments closer to understanding students and inspire improvements; they also provide credibility for program changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use assessment findings to revise curriculum and tasks iteratively
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze assessment results and revise instructional tasks, activity guides, and course delivery to address identified misunderstandings and improve learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: revising tasks on definite integral after interviews, emphasizing writing after baseline data revealed conceptual weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage department-wide periodic meetings and inclusion of students
rubrics_metrics.description: Create formats for periodic meetings where faculty and possible student representatives discuss results and refine issues and questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing discussion sensitizes faculty and students to departmental goals, helps unify the department, and can initiate changes in teaching and assessment practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide departmental supports necessary to accomplish teaching goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify supports the department could provide in an ideal world (e.g., technology, lab space, scheduling, training) to help instructors accomplish teaching goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey invites comments about the 'ideal classroom' and what support would help; responses guide resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate and discuss specific pedagogical techniques with evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the role and effectiveness of pedagogical methods (cooperative groups, projects, student presentations, concrete materials, lecture) and demand solid evidence for claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What solid evidence do you have that these techniques work (or that lecture works)? Use assessment data to support or refute pedagogical choices.
